title: recognize a statistical question (one that anticipates variability in data) among questions that have a single fixed ans
stem: Maya wants to learn about how long it takes students at her school, Kestrel High, to get to school each morning. She plans to collect commute times from a sample of Kestrel students. Which of these is a statistical question that her data could help answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How long did Maya's own commute take this morning?
choices.rationale: This asks about one student on one morning, so the answer is a single value and there is no variability to investigate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: How many students attend Kestrel High?
choices.rationale: Enrollment is one count that can be looked up in a school record, so no variation is anticipated and no sample of students is needed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: What is a typical morning commute time for Kestrel High students, and how much do the times vary from student to student?
choices.rationale: Correct: A statistical question anticipates variability in the data, and only the question about typical commute time and variation among students does; the other three each have a single answer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: What is the speed limit posted on the road in front of Kestrel High?
choices.rationale: The posted limit is a fixed fact printed on a sign, so answering it does not require collecting data that vary.

title: recognize a statistical question (one that anticipates variability in data) among questions that have a single fixed ans (variant 1)
stem: A baker sells cupcakes advertised as weighing 85 grams. She wants to investigate whether that is accurate. Which of these is a statistical question that weighing a sample of her cupcakes could help answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How much does the cupcake on the scale right now weigh?
choices.rationale: This asks about one particular cupcake at one moment, so it has a single answer and no variability to study.

choices.label: B
choices.text: What price is printed on the bakery's cupcake menu?
choices.rationale: A menu price is a fixed fact that is read off the menu, so it is not answered by studying data that vary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Do the cupcakes she sells tend to weigh about 85 grams, and how much do the weights differ from cupcake to cupcake?
choices.rationale: Correct: The question about the typical weight and the differences among cupcakes anticipates variability; the others ask for one measurement, one printed price or one count.

choices.label: D
choices.text: How many cupcakes did the baker bake at 6 a.m. today?
choices.rationale: A count of cupcakes baked at one time is a single number from the baker's records, not a question about variation.

title: recognize a statistical question (one that anticipates variability in data) among questions that have a single fixed ans (variant 2)
stem: A counselor at Ridgeway Middle School wants to learn about the sleep students get on school nights. She will ask a sample of students how long they slept last night. Which of these is a statistical question that the responses could help answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How many hours of sleep did the counselor get last night?
choices.rationale: This concerns one person on one night, so the answer is one value and no variability is anticipated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: How many hours are there between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.?
choices.rationale: The time between two clock times is fixed arithmetic, so no data need to be collected and none vary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: What time does first period begin at Ridgeway?
choices.rationale: A bell schedule is a fixed fact in the school handbook, not something that varies across the students surveyed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: How many hours of sleep do Ridgeway students typically get on a school night, and how do the amounts differ across students?
choices.rationale: Correct: Only the question about typical sleep and differences among students has answers that vary from student to student and so needs data from a sample.

title: recognize a statistical question (one that anticipates variability in data) among questions that have a single fixed ans (variant 3)
stem: A biologist grows tomato plants for 30 days with a new fertilizer and grows other plants without it. Which of these is a statistical question that the plant heights could help answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How tall is the plant in pot 7 today?
choices.rationale: One plant on one day gives a single measurement, so there is no variability to describe or compare.

choices.label: B
choices.text: What is the chemical formula of the main nutrient in the fertilizer?
choices.rationale: A chemical formula is a fixed fact from a reference, not a question whose answer varies from plant to plant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: How many pots are on the greenhouse shelf?
choices.rationale: The number of pots is a single count, so nothing about it varies and no distribution of data is involved.

choices.label: D
choices.text: How do the heights after 30 days of plants grown with the fertilizer compare, in center and spread, with the heights of plants grown without it?
choices.rationale: Correct: Comparing the centers and spreads of two groups of heights anticipates plant-to-plant variability, while each other question has one fixed answer.

title: identify the population of interest from an investigative question and judge what a sample taken from a different group
stem: The Dunmore city council wants to know whether residents support longer public library hours. A researcher stands outside the central library on a Saturday and surveys 150 patrons as they leave; 117 of them say they support longer hours. Which statement correctly identifies the population of interest and what the survey result supports?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The population of interest is all Dunmore residents; the 78% describes only the 150 patrons surveyed and may not represent all residents.
choices.rationale: Correct: 117/150 = 0.78; the question concerns all residents, but the data come only from people who happened to be leaving the library, so 78% is a statistic for that group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The population is the 150 patrons surveyed, so 78% is the exact proportion of the population who support longer hours.
choices.rationale: The 150 patrons are a sample taken from the group the council cares about, not the population, so 78% is not the population proportion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The population is all Dunmore residents, and 78% is a parameter because it describes support among the residents.
choices.rationale: A value computed from a sample is a statistic; a parameter is the value for the whole population, which is unknown here.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is all Dunmore residents, and because 150 is a large sample the 78% can be generalized to every resident.
choices.rationale: A large sample does not fix a sample that was not chosen to represent all residents, since library patrons may differ from other residents.

title: identify the population of interest from an investigative question and judge what a sample taken from a different group  (variant 1)
stem: The principal of Harlow High wants to know whether Harlow students support starting school 30 minutes later. A researcher surveys 60 members of the school's varsity sports teams during practice; 21 of them support the change. Which statement correctly identifies the population of interest and what the survey result supports?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The population is the 60 athletes, so 35% is the exact proportion of Harlow students who support the change.
choices.rationale: The athletes are the sample that was observed, not the population the principal asks about, so 35% is not the school-wide proportion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The population of interest is all Harlow students; the 35% describes only the 60 athletes surveyed and may not represent all students.
choices.rationale: Correct: 21/60 = 0.35; the population is every Harlow student, while the data come from athletes only, so 35% describes that group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The population is all Harlow students, and 35% is a parameter because it describes the opinion of the students.
choices.rationale: A number computed from the 60 athletes is a statistic, and the parameter is the unknown proportion for all students.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is all Harlow students, and because the teams include students from every grade, 35% can be generalized to every student.
choices.rationale: Having every grade represented among athletes does not make them representative of all students on the issue of start times.

title: identify the population of interest from an investigative question and judge what a sample taken from a different group  (variant 2)
stem: A county health office wants to know the typical resting blood pressure of adults in Calloway County. A nurse measures the 200 adults who attend a free health clinic one weekend and finds a mean systolic pressure of 132. Which statement correctly identifies the population of interest and what the result supports?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The population is the 200 adults measured, so 132 is the population mean for the county.
choices.rationale: The 200 adults are the sample, and the county's adults are the population the health office asks about.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The population of interest is all adults in Calloway County; the mean of 132 describes only the 200 clinic attendees and may differ from the county mean.
choices.rationale: Correct: The county mean is a parameter for all adults; 132 is a statistic computed from adults who chose to attend a free clinic, who may not be typical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The population is all adults in the county, and 132 is a parameter because it summarizes their blood pressures.
choices.rationale: A parameter describes the entire population; a mean computed from 200 measured adults is a statistic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is all adults in the county, and since 200 adults were measured, 132 can be generalized to the whole county.
choices.rationale: Sample size cannot repair a sample of people who chose a health clinic, since they may differ from other adults in the county.

title: identify the population of interest from an investigative question and judge what a sample taken from a different group  (variant 3)
stem: A park manager wants to know the typical length of the fish in Lake Verity. An angler uses a net with large mesh, catches 40 fish and measures them, finding a mean length of 31 cm. Which statement correctly identifies the population of interest and what the result supports?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The population is the 40 fish netted, so 31 cm is the mean length of the fish in the lake.
choices.rationale: The netted fish are a sample from the lake's fish, and the manager's question is about all of the fish in the lake.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The population is all the fish in the lake, and 31 cm is a parameter because it describes the fish.
choices.rationale: A mean from the 40 measured fish is a statistic; the lake-wide mean length is the unknown parameter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The population of interest is all the fish in the lake; the 31 cm describes only the 40 fish netted and may overstate the lake's typical length.
choices.rationale: Correct: The question is about every fish in the lake, but a large-mesh net tends to keep only larger fish, so the sample mean of 31 cm may not describe the lake.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is all the fish in the lake, and since 40 fish were measured the 31 cm applies to the whole lake.
choices.rationale: A sample of 40 does not make up for a net that tends to catch larger fish, so the result may not generalize.

title: classify variables in a data set, recognizing numeric identifiers and ordered categories as categorical and counts as qu
stem: A streaming service stores these four items for each subscriber: a 7-digit account ID, a plan tier (Basic, Standard or Premium), the number of hours watched last month, and the number of user profiles on the account. Which choice lists exactly the variables that are quantitative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hours watched last month and number of user profiles.
choices.rationale: Correct: A quantitative variable takes numerical values for which arithmetic such as averaging is meaningful; an ID is a label and a tier is an ordered category, while hours and a count of profiles can be averaged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Account ID, hours watched last month and number of user profiles, because each is recorded as a number.
choices.rationale: An ID number only labels subscribers, so the average of the IDs would be meaningless; being written with digits does not make it quantitative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only hours watched last month, because a count of profiles takes whole-number values and so is categorical.
choices.rationale: A count of profiles is numerical and can be averaged, so it is quantitative even though it takes only whole-number values.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plan tier, hours watched last month and number of user profiles, because the tiers can be put in order.
choices.rationale: A plan tier is a category even though it can be ordered, so it is not quantitative; ordering alone does not make a variable numerical.

title: classify variables in a data set, recognizing numeric identifiers and ordered categories as categorical and counts as qu (variant 1)
stem: A clinic keeps these four items for each patient: a chart number, blood type (A, B, AB or O), resting heart rate in beats per minute, and number of visits last year. Which choice lists exactly the variables that are quantitative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chart number, resting heart rate and number of visits last year, because each is recorded as a number.
choices.rationale: A chart number identifies a patient, so averaging chart numbers is meaningless and the variable is categorical.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only resting heart rate, because visits are counted in whole numbers and so are categorical.
choices.rationale: A count of visits is numerical and averaging counts is meaningful, so it is quantitative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resting heart rate and number of visits last year.
choices.rationale: Correct: Averages make sense for heart rate and for visits, but not for chart numbers, which only identify patients, or for blood types, which are categories.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood type, resting heart rate and number of visits, because blood types can be listed in an order.
choices.rationale: Blood type is a category regardless of any listing order, so it is not quantitative.

title: classify variables in a data set, recognizing numeric identifiers and ordered categories as categorical and counts as qu (variant 2)
stem: A youth league records these four items for each player: jersey number, skill level (Beginner, Intermediate or Advanced), minutes played in the last game, and number of fouls committed. Which choice lists exactly the variables that are quantitative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jersey number, minutes played and number of fouls, because each is written as a number.
choices.rationale: A jersey number only labels a player, so the average jersey number says nothing and the variable is categorical.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only minutes played, because fouls are counted in whole numbers and so are categorical.
choices.rationale: Fouls are a count, and counts are quantitative because their sums and averages are meaningful.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Skill level, minutes played and number of fouls, because the levels are ordered from low to high.
choices.rationale: Skill level places players in ordered categories, but it is not recorded as a numerical amount, so it is categorical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minutes played and number of fouls committed.
choices.rationale: Correct: A jersey number labels a player and skill level is an ordered category; minutes and fouls are numerical measures that can be averaged.

title: classify variables in a data set, recognizing numeric identifiers and ordered categories as categorical and counts as qu (variant 3)
stem: A car lot records these four items for each used car: a five-digit stock number, body style (sedan, SUV or truck), mileage on the odometer, and number of previous owners. Which choice lists exactly the variables that are quantitative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mileage and number of previous owners.
choices.rationale: Correct: Mileage and the count of owners can be averaged meaningfully, whereas a stock number is an identifier and body style is a category.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stock number, mileage and number of previous owners, because each is recorded as a number.
choices.rationale: A stock number labels a car, so arithmetic on stock numbers has no meaning and the variable is categorical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only mileage, because the number of previous owners takes whole-number values and so is categorical.
choices.rationale: A count of owners is quantitative, because it is numerical and its average can be interpreted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Body style, mileage and number of previous owners, because the styles are listed in the order the lot sells them.
choices.rationale: A body style is a category of car, and listing categories in some order does not make it a number.

title: identify the individuals and the type of each variable in a described data set, where one variable summarizes many subje
stem: A researcher records data on 45 hospitals in a state. For each hospital she records its county, its number of beds, and the percentage of its patients who were readmitted within 30 days. Which statement correctly describes the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The individuals are the hospitals; county is categorical, and number of beds and percentage readmitted are quantitative.
choices.rationale: Correct: One row describes each hospital, so hospitals are the individuals; a county name is a category, while a bed count and a percentage readmitted are numerical values that can be averaged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The individuals are the patients; county is categorical, and number of beds and percentage readmitted are quantitative.
choices.rationale: The rows of data describe hospitals, and the patients are only summarized within each hospital, so they are not the individuals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The individuals are the hospitals; county and number of beds are categorical, and only percentage readmitted is quantitative.
choices.rationale: The number of beds is a count and is numerical, so it is quantitative; being a count does not make it a category.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The individuals are the hospitals; county and number of beds are quantitative, and percentage readmitted is categorical because each patient was either readmitted or not.
choices.rationale: The data value recorded for each hospital is a percentage, which is numerical, even though each patient's own outcome was yes or no.

title: identify the individuals and the type of each variable in a described data set, where one variable summarizes many subje (variant 1)
stem: A researcher records data on 32 lakes. For each lake she records the state it lies in, its surface area in acres, and the percentage of fish sampled that had detectable mercury. Which statement correctly describes the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The individuals are the fish sampled; state is categorical, and surface area and percentage with mercury are quantitative.
choices.rationale: The fish are only summarized within each lake, so the lakes, and not the fish, are the individuals described by each row.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The individuals are the lakes; state is categorical, and surface area and percentage with mercury are quantitative.
choices.rationale: Correct: Each row is a lake, so lakes are the individuals; state names are categories, while an area and a percentage are numerical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The individuals are the lakes; state and surface area are categorical, and only the percentage with mercury is quantitative.
choices.rationale: Surface area is a measured amount that can be averaged, so it is quantitative rather than categorical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The individuals are the lakes; state and surface area are quantitative, and the percentage with mercury is categorical because each fish either had mercury or did not.
choices.rationale: The value recorded for each lake is a percentage, which is numerical, even though each fish was classified yes or no.

title: identify the individuals and the type of each variable in a described data set, where one variable summarizes many subje (variant 2)
stem: A state agency records data on 28 school districts. For each district it records the region (North, South, East or West), the number of students enrolled, and the percentage of students who graduated within four years. Which statement correctly describes the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The individuals are the students; region is categorical, and enrollment and graduation percentage are quantitative.
choices.rationale: Students appear only through the district totals, so they are not the individuals that the rows describe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The individuals are the districts; region and enrollment are categorical, and only graduation percentage is quantitative.
choices.rationale: Enrollment is a count that can be averaged across districts, so it is quantitative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The individuals are the districts; region and enrollment are quantitative, and graduation percentage is categorical because each student either graduated or did not.
choices.rationale: A district's graduation percentage is a number, and the yes-or-no outcome of each student does not make this variable categorical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The individuals are the districts; region is categorical, and enrollment and graduation percentage are quantitative.
choices.rationale: Correct: One row describes each district, so districts are the individuals; a region is a category, and enrollment and a percentage are numerical.

title: identify the individuals and the type of each variable in a described data set, where one variable summarizes many subje (variant 3)
stem: An airport analyst records data on 36 flights on one day. For each flight she records the airline, the number of passengers, and the percentage of the scheduled seats that were filled. Which statement correctly describes the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The individuals are the airlines; airline is categorical, and number of passengers and percentage of seats filled are quantitative.
choices.rationale: Several flights belong to the same airline, so an airline is a category of the flights and is not the individual described by each row.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The individuals are the flights; airline and number of passengers are categorical, and only percentage of seats filled is quantitative.
choices.rationale: A passenger count is numerical and can be averaged over flights, so it is quantitative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The individuals are the flights; airline is categorical, and number of passengers and percentage of seats filled are quantitative.
choices.rationale: Correct: Each row is one flight, so flights are the individuals; an airline name is a category, while a passenger count and a percentage are numerical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The individuals are the flights; airline and number of passengers are quantitative, and percentage of seats filled is categorical because each seat was either filled or empty.
choices.rationale: The value recorded for each flight is a percentage, which is numerical, even though each seat was either filled or empty.

title: use a relative frequency and a count to recover the total of a categorical table, then find a conditional percentage amo
stem: In a survey about how they usually get to school, 27 students chose the bus, which was 18% of all students surveyed. Another 34% of all students surveyed chose a car. Among the students who did NOT choose the bus, what percent chose a car, to the nearest tenth of a percent?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: 27/0.18 = 150 students; 0.34(150) = 51 car riders; 150 − 27 = 123 non-bus students; 51/123 = 0.415.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 34% is the percent of all 150 students who chose a car, and the question restricts attention to the 123 who did not choose the bus.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Adding 18% and 34% combines the bus and car percentages, which does not answer a question about cars among non-bus riders.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 51 is the number of car riders, not a percent, and it has not been divided by the 123 students in the group.

title: use a relative frequency and a count to recover the total of a categorical table, then find a conditional percentage amo (variant 1)
stem: An online pizzeria recorded the orders placed in one week. There were 45 delivery orders, which was 15% of all orders, and 40% of all orders were for pickup. Among the orders that were NOT for delivery, what percent were for pickup, to the nearest tenth of a percent?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 40% is the share of all 300 orders; the question is about the 255 orders that were not for delivery.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Adding 15% and 40% does not describe pickup orders within the non-delivery group.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: 45/0.15 = 300 orders; 0.40(300) = 120 pickup orders; 300 − 45 = 255 non-delivery orders; 120/255 = 0.471.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 85% is the share of all orders that were not for delivery, not the share of those orders that were for pickup.

title: use a relative frequency and a count to recover the total of a categorical table, then find a conditional percentage amo (variant 2)
stem: A librarian recorded the favorite genre of each student in a reading survey. Mystery was chosen by 18 students, which was 12% of all students surveyed, and fantasy was chosen by 28% of all students surveyed. Among the students who did NOT choose mystery, what percent chose fantasy, to the nearest tenth of a percent?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 28% is the share of all 150 students and ignores the condition that the student did not choose mystery.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Adding 12% and 28% combines two categories and does not answer the question about fantasy among non-mystery students.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 42 is the number of students who chose fantasy, not a percent, and it has not been divided by the 132 non-mystery students.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: 18/0.12 = 150 students; 0.28(150) = 42 fantasy fans; 150 − 18 = 132 non-mystery students; 42/132 = 0.318.

title: use a relative frequency and a count to recover the total of a categorical table, then find a conditional percentage amo (variant 3)
stem: In a survey of pet ownership, 30 students said cat, which was 20% of all students surveyed, and 38% of all students surveyed said dog. Among the students who did NOT say cat, what percent said something other than dog, to the nearest tenth of a percent?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 47.5% is the percent of the non-cat students who said dog, the complement of what was asked.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 62% is the percent of all 150 students who did not say dog, which ignores the condition that the student did not say cat.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 80% is the percent of all students who did not say cat, which is not a percent of that group that avoided dog.

title: compare two groups of different sizes using relative frequencies, and distinguish a difference in percentage points from
stem: Two towns were surveyed about a proposed park. In Town A, 120 of the 400 residents surveyed supported the plan. In Town B, 90 of the 225 residents surveyed supported it. Which statement about the survey results is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Support is stronger in Town A, because 120 supporters is more than 90 supporters.
choices.rationale: Counts depend on how many people were surveyed, so more supporters in Town A comes from the larger group surveyed and does not show stronger support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A larger share of the Town B residents surveyed supported the plan, 40% compared with 30%, even though Town A had more supporters.
choices.rationale: Correct: Relative frequencies are 120/400 = 30% and 90/225 = 40%; the gap is 10 percentage points, while 40/30 is about a 33% relative increase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The towns cannot be compared, because different numbers of residents were surveyed in each.
choices.rationale: Relative frequencies adjust for different group sizes, so proportions can be compared even when the numbers surveyed differ.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Support in Town B is 10% greater than in Town A, because 40% minus 30% is 10%.
choices.rationale: The 10 is a difference in percentage points; Town B's share is about 33% greater in relative terms, so 10% misdescribes the comparison.

title: compare two groups of different sizes using relative frequencies, and distinguish a difference in percentage points from (variant 1)
stem: A district asked students at two schools whether they prefer an online option for a course. At School X, 84 of the 240 students asked said yes. At School Y, 60 of the 120 students asked said yes. Which statement about the results is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A larger share of the School Y students asked preferred the online option, 50% compared with 35%, even though School X had more students saying yes.
choices.rationale: Correct: The shares are 84/240 = 35% and 60/120 = 50%; the gap is 15 percentage points, and 50/35 is a relative increase of about 43%.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preference is stronger at School X, because 84 students is more than 60 students.
choices.rationale: More yes answers at School X come from asking twice as many students, which does not show that a larger share preferred the option.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The schools cannot be compared, because a different number of students was asked at each.
choices.rationale: Percentages put the schools on a common scale, so they can be compared even though the group sizes differ.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preference at School Y is 15% greater than at School X, because 50% minus 35% is 15%.
choices.rationale: A gap of 15 is in percentage points; School Y's share is about 43% greater in relative terms, so saying 15% greater misdescribes it.

title: compare two groups of different sizes using relative frequencies, and distinguish a difference in percentage points from (variant 2)
stem: A city surveyed residents of two wards about a new recycling schedule. In Ward 1, 66 of the 300 residents surveyed favored it. In Ward 2, 40 of the 160 residents surveyed favored it. Which statement about the results is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Favor is higher in Ward 1, because 66 people is more than 40 people.
choices.rationale: Ward 1 has more people in favor only because more residents were surveyed there; the counts do not compare the shares.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A larger share of the Ward 2 residents surveyed favored the schedule, 25% compared with 22%, even though Ward 1 had more people in favor.
choices.rationale: Correct: The shares are 66/300 = 22% and 40/160 = 25%; the gap is 3 percentage points, and 25/22 is a relative increase of about 14%.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The wards cannot be compared, because the numbers of residents surveyed were not equal.
choices.rationale: Proportions allow groups of unequal size to be compared fairly, so unequal numbers surveyed do not prevent a comparison.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Favor in Ward 2 is 3% greater than in Ward 1, because 25% minus 22% is 3%.
choices.rationale: A gap of 3 is in percentage points; Ward 2's share is about 14% greater in relative terms, so saying 3% greater is a misreading.

title: compare two groups of different sizes using relative frequencies, and distinguish a difference in percentage points from (variant 3)
stem: A school surveyed two grades about a later start time. In Grade 9, 52 of the 130 students surveyed said yes. In Grade 10, 78 of the 260 students surveyed said yes. Which statement about the results is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Support is stronger in Grade 10, because 78 students is more than 52 students.
choices.rationale: More yes answers in Grade 10 come from surveying twice as many students and do not show that a larger share supported the change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The grades cannot be compared, because a different number of students was surveyed in each grade.
choices.rationale: Using percentages removes the effect of different group sizes, so the grades can be compared directly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A larger share of the Grade 9 students surveyed said yes, 40% compared with 30%, even though Grade 10 had more students saying yes.
choices.rationale: Correct: The shares are 52/130 = 40% and 78/260 = 30%; the gap is 10 percentage points, and 40/30 is a relative increase of about 33%.

choices.label: D

title: evaluate a claim drawn from a bar chart whose vertical axis does not start at zero, comparing visual height with the act
stem: A bar chart shows the number of complaints received by two branches of a bank last month. The vertical axis starts at 40 instead of 0. The bar for Branch 1 reaches 46 complaints and the bar for Branch 2 reaches 52 complaints. A viewer says, "Branch 2's bar is twice as tall as Branch 1's, so Branch 2 had twice as many complaints." Which statement best evaluates the claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because the bar for Branch 2 is twice as tall and the height of a bar shows how many times larger a count is.

choices.text: The claim is incorrect: the axis starts at 40, so the visible bar heights are 6 and 12, but Branch 2 had 52 complaints compared with 46, about 13% more.

choices.rationale: The difference of 6 complaints is not a percent; as a fraction of Branch 1's 46 complaints, it is about 13%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is incorrect: Branch 1 had about 13% more complaints than Branch 2, because 52 divided by 46 is about 1.13.
choices.rationale: 52/46 compares Branch 2 to Branch 1, so Branch 2, not Branch 1, had the larger count and the percent increase is for Branch 2.

title: choose a display for a categorical variable that allows multiple responses, recognizing when a pie chart is inappropriat
stem: A survey of 200 students asked them to mark every after-school activity they take part in. The results: sports 120 students, music 90, art 70 and coding 50 (students could mark more than one). choices.label: D
choices.text: A pie chart with slices proportional to the counts 120, 90, 70 and 50, which total 330.
choices.rationale: A pie of the 330 marks shows each activity's share of all marks, not the percent of the 200 students who do each activity, so it does not answer the question.

title: choose the description of a quantitative distribution that has shape, resistant center and spread, and unusual features,
stem: The annual salaries, in thousands of dollars, of the 38 employees of a small firm form a distribution with these features: most salaries are between 42 and 78, with a single peak, a median of 57, Q1 = 50 and Q3 = 64; two employees earn about 140 and 155, far above everyone else; the mean is about 63 and the standard deviation about 22. Which is the best description of the distribution of salaries?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The salaries are roughly symmetric and centered near $63 thousand, and they typically vary from the center by about $22 thousand.
choices.rationale: The mean and standard deviation are pulled up by the two high salaries, and the description ignores that outliers make the shape skewed to the right.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distribution is skewed right, with a median of 57 and an interquartile range of 14.
choices.rationale: This gives shape, center and spread but with no units or context and no mention of the two unusually high salaries, so it is not a complete description in context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The salaries are skewed to the right by two high outliers (about $140 thousand and $155 thousand); the typical salary is about $57 thousand, and the middle 50% span about $14 thousand.
choices.rationale: Correct: IQR = 64 − 50 = 14, and the fence 64 + 1.5(14) = 85 is below 140 and 155, so they are outliers; they pull the mean (63) above the median (57), so median and IQR describe the center and spread.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The salaries are bimodal, with one peak near $57 thousand and a second peak near $150 thousand.
choices.rationale: Two isolated values do not form a second peak; they are unusual values (outliers) in a distribution that has one peak.

title: choose the description of a quantitative distribution that has shape, resistant center and spread, and unusual features, (variant 3)
stem: The heights of 40 adult visitors to a gym form a distribution with these features: a single peak, symmetric and mound-shaped, with mean 72 inches, standard deviation about 3 inches, Q1 = 70 and Q3 = 74; the smallest height is 65 and the largest is 79. Which is the best description of the distribution of heights?

stem: A teacher plots the exam scores of her 30 students. The histogram has two separate peaks, one near 60 and one near 90, with about 15 students at each peak and almost no scores between 70 and 80. The mean score is 75. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean of 75 describes a typical student well, because the mean is the center of the distribution and most students scored near it.
choices.rationale: A mean can fall in a region with almost no data, and here few students are near 75, so it does not represent a typical score.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the distribution has two peaks, it must be skewed, so the median should be reported in place of the mean.
choices.rationale: A bimodal distribution with equal peaks is not skewed, and neither the mean nor the median would describe the two groups well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean of 75 is a poor description of a typical student, because almost no one scored near 75; the class seems to consist of two groups that should be described separately.
choices.rationale: Correct: Half of the scores cluster near 60 and half near 90, so the mean (75) lies in the gap where almost no student scored and is not a typical value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two peaks are outliers, so they should be removed before the class scores are described.
choices.rationale: The peaks contain all of the students, so they are the main feature of the data and not unusual individual values to delete.

title: determine how a linear change of units (multiply then add) changes the mean and standard deviation.
stem: A test is scored out of 50 points. The raw scores x have mean 31 and standard deviation 4.5. The teacher reports each student's percent score as y = 2x + 5. Which choice gives the mean and standard deviation of the reported scores y?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean 67 and standard deviation 14
choices.rationale: Adding 5 shifts every score and does not change the spread, so the standard deviation is 2(4.5) = 9, not 9 + 5.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean 67 and standard deviation 9
choices.rationale: Correct: The mean is transformed like each value, 2(31) + 5 = 67; the standard deviation is multiplied by |2| and unaffected by adding 5, so it is 2(4.5) = 9.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean 62 and standard deviation 9
choices.rationale: The mean must also reflect the added 5 points, so it is 2(31) + 5 = 67 and not 2(31) = 62.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean 36 and standard deviation 9.5
choices.rationale: This applies only the addition and ignores the multiplication by 2, which doubles both the center and the spread.

title: determine how a linear change of units (multiply then add) changes the mean and standard deviation. (variant 1)
stem: Daily high temperatures in a city, in degrees Celsius C, have mean 21 and standard deviation 3. Each temperature is converted to degrees Fahrenheit using F = 1.8C + 32. Which choice gives the mean and standard deviation of the temperatures in Fahrenheit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean 69.8 and standard deviation 5.4
choices.rationale: Correct: Mean: 1.8(21) + 32 = 69.8; standard deviation: 1.8(3) = 5.4, since adding 32 does not change the spread.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean 69.8 and standard deviation 37.4
choices.rationale: Adding 32 shifts all the temperatures by the same amount and leaves the spread unchanged, so the standard deviation is 1.8(3) = 5.4.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean 37.8 and standard deviation 5.4
choices.rationale: The mean also gets the 32 added, so the mean is 1.8(21) + 32 = 69.8 and not just 1.8(21).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean 53 and standard deviation 35
choices.rationale: This adds 32 to the mean and the standard deviation and ignores the multiplication by 1.8 that rescales both.

title: determine how a linear change of units (multiply then add) changes the mean and standard deviation. (variant 2)
stem: The hours worked in a week by the employees of a shop have median 34 hours and IQR 6 hours. Each employee's weekly pay, in dollars, is y = 15x + 40, where x is hours worked. Which choice gives the median and IQR of the weekly pay?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Median 550 dollars and IQR 130 dollars
choices.rationale: The fixed 40 raises every pay amount equally, so it does not change the IQR, which is 15(6) = 90.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Median 510 dollars and IQR 90 dollars
choices.rationale: The median is also raised by the 40, so it is 15(34) + 40 = 550 and not 15(34) = 510.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Median 550 dollars and IQR 90 dollars
choices.rationale: Correct: Median: 15(34) + 40 = 550; IQR: 15(6) = 90, because adding the fixed 40 does not change the distance between the quartiles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Median 74 dollars and IQR 46 dollars
choices.rationale: This only adds 40 to each summary and leaves out the multiplication by 15 that rescales both the center and the spread.

title: determine how a linear change of units (multiply then add) changes the mean and standard deviation. (variant 3)
stem: A quiz deducts 4 points for each error from a starting score of 100, so the score is y = 100 − 4x, where x is the number of errors. The numbers of errors have mean 6.5 and standard deviation 2.5. Which choice gives the mean and standard deviation of the quiz scores?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean 74 and standard deviation 10
choices.rationale: Correct: Mean: 100 − 4(6.5) = 74; standard deviation: |−4|(2.5) = 10, since a standard deviation cannot be negative and adding 100 does not change it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean 74 and standard deviation −10
choices.rationale: A standard deviation is a nonnegative measure of spread, so multiplying by −4 gives 4(2.5) = 10 and not a negative number.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean 93.5 and standard deviation 10
choices.rationale: The mean must reflect both the multiplication by −4 and the 100 points, so it is 100 − 4(6.5) = 74.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean 74 and standard deviation 90
choices.rationale: The 100 shifts every score and leaves the spread unchanged, so the standard deviation is 10 and not 100 − 10.

title: find and interpret the mean of a combined group from the means and sizes of two subgroups, avoiding the unweighted avera
stem: Section 1 of a course has 12 students with a mean quiz score of 85, and Section 2 has 28 students with a mean quiz score of 75. The scores from both sections are combined. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The combined mean is 80, the average of 85 and 75.
choices.rationale: Averaging 85 and 75 gives each section equal weight, but Section 2 has more than twice as many students and so counts more.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The combined mean cannot be found without knowing the individual scores.
choices.rationale: The sum of each section's scores is its mean times its size, so the combined mean can be computed from the means and sizes alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The combined mean is 78, which is closer to 75 because Section 2 has more students.
choices.rationale: Correct: Total points = 12(85) + 28(75) = 1020 + 2100 = 3120, and 3120/40 = 78; each mean is weighted by its number of students.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The combined mean is 78, and the combined median must also be 78.
choices.rationale: The mean is 78, but the median of the combined scores cannot be determined from the means and sizes, and it need not equal the mean.

title: find and interpret the mean of a combined group from the means and sizes of two subgroups, avoiding the unweighted avera (variant 1)
stem: A factory has two production lines. Line 1 has 18 machines with a mean output of 240 units per day, and Line 2 has 42 machines with a mean output of 200 units per day. Which statement about the mean output of all 60 machines is correct?

choices.rationale: The simple average of 240 and 200 gives the two lines equal weight, but Line 2 has more than twice as many machines.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mean output of all 60 machines cannot be found without the output of each machine.
choices.rationale: Each line's total output is its mean times its number of machines, so the overall mean can be found from the given means and sizes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean output of all 60 machines is 212 units, and the median output of all 60 machines must also be 212.
choices.rationale: The mean is 212, but the combined median cannot be determined from the means and sizes and need not equal the mean.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean output of all 60 machines is 212 units, which is closer to 200 because Line 2 has more machines.

title: find and interpret the mean of a combined group from the means and sizes of two subgroups, avoiding the unweighted avera (variant 2)
stem: A hiking club has 25 members with a mean age of 30 years and 15 guests with a mean age of 50 years. Which statement about the mean age of all 40 people is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean age of all 40 people is 40 years, the average of 30 and 50.
choices.rationale: Averaging 30 and 50 treats the groups as equal in size, but there are 25 members and only 15 guests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mean age of all 40 people cannot be found without the age of each person.
choices.rationale: Each group's total age is its mean times its size, so the overall mean can be calculated from the means and sizes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean age of all 40 people is 37.5 years, and the median age of all 40 people must also be 37.5.
choices.rationale: The mean is 37.5, but the median of the 40 ages cannot be found from the means and sizes and need not equal 37.5.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean age of all 40 people is 37.5 years, which is closer to 30 because the club has more members than guests.

title: find and interpret the mean of a combined group from the means and sizes of two subgroups, avoiding the unweighted avera (variant 3)
stem: Drivers on a highway are grouped by vehicle type. 60% are cars, with a mean speed of 62 miles per hour, and 40% are trucks, with a mean speed of 50 miles per hour. Which statement about the mean speed of all drivers is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean speed of all drivers is 56 miles per hour, the average of 62 and 50.
choices.rationale: The simple average of 62 and 50 ignores that 60% of the drivers are in cars and only 40% are in trucks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mean speed of all drivers is 57.2 miles per hour, which is closer to 62 because more drivers are in cars.
choices.rationale: Correct: Mean = 0.60(62) + 0.40(50) = 37.2 + 20 = 57.2 miles per hour, a weighted mean using the proportion in each group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean speed of all drivers cannot be found without the speed of every driver.
choices.rationale: With the proportion of drivers in each group and each group's mean, the overall mean is a weighted average and can be found.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean speed of all drivers is 57.2 miles per hour, and the median speed of all drivers must also be 57.2.
choices.rationale: The mean is 57.2, but the median of all speeds cannot be found from the group means and proportions and need not equal the mean.
